definition: to say officially what must be done; or, of a doctor, to order a medicine

examples.text: The protocol prescribes a ten-minute wait between doses.
The charter prescribed how the council's members were to be chosen.
The doctor prescribed rest, fluids, and no screens for two days.

confused.note: Prescribe means to order or recommend; proscribe means to forbid.

questions.passage: The building code does not leave such matters to chance. It ______ the exact width of every staircase, the height of every railing, and the number of exits each floor must have.
questions.explanation: Setting exact required measurements is stating officially what must be done.

distractors.why: Proscribes means forbids; the code is requiring these features, not banning them.
Hampers means hinders, which does not fit setting requirements.
Fathoms means understands, which does not fit.

definition: most common, noticeable, or powerful

examples.text: Nitrogen is the predominant gas in Earth's atmosphere.
Wool was the predominant export of the kingdom for three centuries.
Blue is the predominant color in my closet, mostly by accident.

confused.note: Predominant means most common or strongest; preeminent means most distinguished.

questions.passage: Several languages are spoken in the valley, but one is clearly ______. More than four in five residents use it at home, and it is the language of every shop sign and school lesson.
questions.explanation: A language used by four in five residents is the most common.

distractors.why: Indiscriminate means not making careful choices, which does not describe a language.
Penitent means remorseful, which does not fit.
Static means unchanging, which is not what the statistics show.

definition: made up of parts or members that are all of the same kind

examples.text: Stir until the mixture is homogeneous, with no visible lumps.
The island's population was unusually homogeneous until the port opened.
The neighborhood is homogeneous: every house is the same shade of beige.

confused.note: Homogeneous (five syllables) is the standard spelling for "all of one kind."

questions.passage: Critics complained that the anthology was too ______. All thirty of its poets had attended the same university, lived in the same city, and written in the same spare, ironic style.
questions.explanation: Poets alike in schooling, home, and style make a collection all of one kind.

distractors.why: Eclectic means drawn from varied sources, the opposite of this anthology.
Irreverent means disrespectful, which is not the complaint.
Uncanny means strangely mysterious, which does not fit.

definition: a person who argues in favor of something

examples.text: She was an early proponent of free public libraries.
Proponents of the theory point to the fossil evidence.
My dad is a proponent of the nine o'clock bedtime, even on weekends.

confused.note: A proponent argues for something; an opponent argues against it.

questions.passage: The mayor is a longtime ______ of bicycle commuting. She has tripled the number of bike lanes, rides to work herself, and argues in every budget debate for more spending on cycling.
questions.explanation: Building lanes and arguing for cycling make her a supporter.

distractors.why: A novice is a beginner, which a longtime cyclist is not.
An opponent argues against something, the opposite of her position.
A stimulus is something that prompts a response, not a person who supports a cause.

definition: allowing someone to have or do whatever they want; lenient

examples.text: The indulgent grandfather slips the children sweets when their mother looks away.
The indulgent regent let the young king skip every council meeting.
My indulgent aunt lets us stay up until midnight when we visit.

confused.note: Indulgent means lenient; indigent means poor.

questions.passage: The school's previous head had enforced every rule to the letter. Her successor was far more ______, overlooking late homework, allowing students to eat in class, and rarely sending anyone to detention.
questions.explanation: Overlooking rule-breaking shows a lenient attitude.

distractors.why: Decorous means proper and polite, which is not the contrast with strict enforcement.
Strident means loud and harsh, which does not fit.
Penitent means remorseful, which does not fit.

definition: done without careful thought or choice, often causing harm

examples.text: The indiscriminate use of antibiotics has produced resistant bacteria.
The army's indiscriminate burning of villages turned the countryside against it.
My indiscriminate clicking on pop-up ads gave the laptop a virus.

confused.note: Indiscriminate means not choosing carefully; indiscreet means careless about keeping secrets.

questions.passage: Early pesticides were ______ in their effects. They killed the insects that damaged crops but also the bees that pollinated them and the birds that fed on both.
questions.explanation: Killing helpful and harmful species alike is acting without distinction.

distractors.why: Selective means choosing carefully, the opposite of killing everything.
Decorous means proper, which does not describe a pesticide.
Fundamental means basic, which does not fit.

definition: to become weaker or smaller from lack of use

examples.text: Muscles atrophy quickly when a limb is kept in a cast.
The city's shipbuilding skills atrophied during the long peace.
My Spanish has atrophied since I stopped practicing.

confused.note: Atrophy means to waste away; a trophy is a prize.

questions.passage: Astronauts on long missions must exercise for two hours every day. Without the constant pull of gravity, their leg muscles would otherwise ______, leaving them unable to walk when they returned to Earth.
questions.explanation: Unused muscles weaken and shrink.

distractors.why: Clamor means to demand noisily, which muscles cannot do.
Supplant means to replace, which does not fit.
Decry means to condemn, which does not fit.

definition: not showing the respect that is expected, often in a humorous way

examples.text: The irreverent narrator refers to the king as "that old pudding."
Irreverent cartoons of the bishop circulated through the city.
My brother's irreverent toast at the wedding made even Grandma laugh.

confused.note: Irreverent means lacking respect; irrelevant means not related to the matter.

questions.passage: The guidebook takes an ______ approach to the city's monuments. It describes the grand cathedral as "a very large place to get out of the rain" and the national museum as "three floors of other people's furniture."
questions.explanation: Joking descriptions of revered monuments show a playful lack of respect.

distractors.why: Decorous means proper and dignified, the opposite of these jokes.
Penitent means remorseful, which does not fit.
Predominant means most common, which does not describe an approach.

partsNote: from Latin vereri, "to fear, to respect"

definition: excessive admiration or praise

examples.text: The general returned to the adulation of crowds that had forgotten his defeats.
The young actress is not prepared for the adulation that follows her first film.
The goalie accepted the adulation of the fans with an embarrassed wave.

confused.note: Adulation is excessive praise; adulteration is making something impure.

questions.passage: The singer grew uncomfortable with the ______ of her fans. They camped outside her house, copied her clothes, and treated her most casual remark as if it were wisdom.
questions.explanation: Camping out and treating every remark as wisdom is excessive admiration.

distractors.why: An altercation is a noisy argument, which does not describe the fans' devotion.
A hierarchy is a system of ranks, which does not fit.
A dilemma is a difficult choice, which does not fit.

definition: to say publicly and strongly that something is wrong

examples.text: Reformers decried the use of child labor in the mills.
The essayist decries the decline of letter writing.
The coach decried the state of the field, which was mostly mud.

confused.note: To decry is to condemn; to descry is to catch sight of.

questions.passage: Teachers' unions ______ the proposed budget, which would have eliminated music and art classes in forty schools. Their leaders called it "an attack on childhood" and urged parents to protest.
questions.explanation: Calling the budget an attack and urging protest is strong public condemnation.

distractors.why: Fathomed means understood, which does not capture their opposition.
Prescribed means ordered or recommended, which is not what the unions did.
Abetted means helped, the opposite of opposing the budget.

partsNote: from Old French crier, "to cry": to cry down

definition: feeling or showing sorrow for having done wrong

examples.text: The penitent thief returns the silver and asks only to be forgiven.
Penitent pilgrims walked barefoot to the shrine.
My penitent little brother offered me his dessert after breaking my headphones.

confused.note: Penitent means remorseful; pertinent means relevant.

questions.passage: The judge noted that the young man seemed genuinely ______. He had confessed before he was suspected, repaid what he had taken, and volunteered each weekend at the shop he had robbed.
questions.explanation: Confessing, repaying, and volunteering show sincere remorse.

distractors.why: Irreverent means disrespectful, which his conduct was not.
Incorrigible means beyond reform, the opposite of someone making amends.
Indulgent means lenient, which describes a judge's attitude, not the young man's remorse.

definition: to take the place of something or someone, often by force or over time

examples.text: Steam ships gradually supplanted sailing vessels on the Atlantic routes.
The invasive grass has supplanted native plants along the river.
Texting has almost entirely supplanted phone calls among my friends.

confused.note: To supplant is to replace; to supplement is to add to.

questions.passage: For most of the century, radio was the country's main source of news. By the 1960s it had been ______ by television, which could show viewers the events that radio could only describe.
questions.explanation: Television took radio's place.

distractors.why: Supplemented means added to; the passage says radio lost its place, not that it gained a partner.
Prescribed means ordered, which does not fit.
Hampered means hindered; radio was replaced as the main source, not merely slowed.

partsNote: from Latin plantare, "to plant": to trip up from below

definition: polite, calm, and proper in behavior

examples.text: The decorous guests pretend not to notice the host's torn sleeve.
Debates in the old chamber were decorous, with members bowing before they spoke.
The usually rowdy team was surprisingly decorous at the awards dinner.

confused.note: Decorous means proper in behavior; decorative means ornamental.

questions.passage: Those who expected shouting at the town meeting were disappointed. The discussion was entirely ______: speakers waited their turn, addressed one another as "my neighbor," and thanked the chair before sitting down.
questions.explanation: Waiting turns and courteous address show polite, proper behavior.

distractors.why: Strident means loud and harsh, which is what some expected.
Indiscriminate means unselective, which does not describe a polite discussion.
Uncanny means eerily strange, which does not fit.

definition: quick to notice and understand things that are not obvious

examples.text: The perspicacious governess sees at once which child broke the vase.
A perspicacious envoy noticed that the king never ate from his own plate.
My perspicacious grandmother can tell from one "hello" that something is wrong.

confused.note: Perspicacious describes a person with sharp insight; perspicuous describes writing that is clear.

questions.passage: Most readers took the memoir at face value. One ______ reviewer, however, noticed that the dates in three chapters could not all be true and correctly guessed that parts of the story had been invented.
questions.explanation: Noticing a subtle inconsistency that others missed shows sharp insight.

distractors.why: Indulgent means lenient, which would not lead a reviewer to catch errors.
Penitent means remorseful, which does not fit.
Static means unchanging, which does not describe a reviewer.

definition: strange and hard to explain, often in a slightly frightening way

examples.text: The twins have an uncanny habit of finishing each other's sentences.
The robot's face is close enough to human to seem uncanny.
My dog has an uncanny ability to know when I am about to leave.

confused.note: Uncanny means eerily strange; canny means shrewd. They are not opposites.

questions.passage: Sailors spoke of the old pilot's ______ ability to find the harbor in any weather. Even in thick fog, without lights or instruments, he would bring a ship to the dock as if he could see through the mist.
questions.explanation: Navigating blind in fog is a strange, hard-to-explain ability.

distractors.why: Rudimentary means basic and undeveloped, the opposite of such skill.
Decorous means proper, which does not describe an ability.
Homogeneous means all alike, which does not fit.

definition: to understand something difficult after thinking about it

examples.text: The narrator cannot fathom why her sister would leave without a word.
Physicists are only beginning to fathom the nature of dark matter.
I cannot fathom how my brother loses one sock from every pair.

confused.note: To fathom is to understand; a phantom is a ghost.

questions.passage: The explorers could not ______ how the ancient builders had moved stones weighing forty tons across a hundred miles of desert. No road, sledge, or harbor had ever been found.
questions.explanation: They could not understand how it was done.

distractors.why: Decry means to condemn, which is not their reaction.
Supplant means to replace, which does not fit.
Prohibit means to forbid, which does not fit.

definition: a loud, continuous noise, especially of people shouting or demanding something

examples.text: The clamor for bread outside the palace grew louder each day.
Above the clamor of the market, the boy hears his name.
The clamor in the cafeteria makes conversation impossible.

confused.note: Clamor is loud noise or demand; glamour is attractive charm.

questions.passage: When the factory's owners announced that wages would be cut, the ______ from workers was immediate. Hundreds gathered at the gates, shouting and beating on the iron bars, and the noise could be heard across the river.
questions.explanation: Hundreds shouting at the gates produce a loud, sustained outcry.

distractors.why: Adulation is excessive praise, the opposite of angry protest.
A stimulus is something that prompts a reaction, not the noisy reaction itself.
A culmination is a final high point, which does not describe an immediate outcry.

definition: forming the base from which everything else develops; of central importance

examples.text: The cell is the fundamental unit of life.
The charter guaranteed the fundamental right to a fair trial.
A fundamental rule of cooking: read the whole recipe first.

confused.note: Fundamental means basic; a fundamentalist holds strictly to a set of beliefs.

questions.passage: The engineers concluded that the bridge's problems could not be fixed with patches. The flaw was ______: the original design had placed the supports on soil too soft to bear the load.
questions.explanation: A flaw in the original design lies at the base of everything else.

distractors.why: Superficial means only on the surface, the opposite of a flaw in the foundations.
Posthumous means happening after death, which does not fit.
Uncanny means eerily strange, which does not describe a design flaw.

definition: important and well known; or easily seen

examples.text: Several prominent merchants signed the petition against the tax.
The scar is still prominent on the mountainside decades after the landslide.
The trophy sits in a prominent spot on the mantel.

confused.note: Prominent means well known or noticeable; preeminent means the very best in a field.

questions.passage: The committee wanted its report to be signed by someone ______. It chose a retired astronaut whose name was known in every household and whose opinion newspapers were certain to quote.
questions.explanation: A person known in every household is well known and important.

distractors.why: Obscure means little known, the opposite of a household name.
Penitent means remorseful, which is not what the committee wanted.
Indulgent means lenient, which does not fit.

definition: not moving, changing, or developing

examples.text: Unlike a river, the lake's water level is nearly static through the year.
The village population remained static for two centuries.
My bank balance has been static since I stopped babysitting.

confused.note: Static means unchanging; stoic means enduring hardship without complaint.

questions.passage: Language is never ______. New words enter every year, old ones fade, and meanings drift so steadily that a text written five centuries ago can be hard for a modern reader to follow.
questions.explanation: Constant change in words and meanings means language does not stay fixed.

distractors.why: Dynamic means constantly changing; "never dynamic" would contradict the examples.
Prominent means well known or noticeable, which does not fit.
Decorous means proper, which does not fit.

definition: something that causes a reaction or encourages activity

examples.text: The plant bends toward light, its response to a stimulus from one side.
Cheap land was a powerful stimulus to settlement in the west.
The smell of coffee is the only stimulus that gets my dad out of bed.

confused.note: A stimulus is anything that provokes a response; a stimulant is a substance that raises alertness.

questions.passage: Economists disagree about whether the tax cut will work as a ______. Its supporters say it will encourage companies to hire; its critics predict that firms will simply keep the extra money.
questions.explanation: A measure meant to encourage hiring is something that prompts activity.

distractors.why: A hierarchy is a ranking system, which does not fit.
A deterrent discourages activity, the opposite of what supporters expect.
A clamor is a loud outcry, which does not fit.

definition: a system in which people or things are arranged in levels of importance

examples.text: Wolves live in packs with a clear hierarchy.
The church's hierarchy ran from village priest to pope.
There is a strict hierarchy on the school bus: seniors in the back.

confused.note: A hierarchy is an ordered system of ranks; anarchy is the absence of any ruling order.

questions.passage: The restaurant's kitchen runs on a rigid ______. Dishwashers answer to line cooks, line cooks to the sous-chef, and the sous-chef to the head chef, whose word on any matter is final.
questions.explanation: Each level answering to the one above is a system of ranks.

distractors.why: A dilemma is a difficult choice, not a chain of command.
An altercation is a quarrel, which does not fit.
Adulation is excessive praise, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Greek hieros, "sacred," and archein, "to rule"

definition: a situation in which a difficult choice must be made between two options

examples.text: The heroine's dilemma is whether to keep her promise or save her brother.
The council faced a dilemma: raise taxes or abandon the harbor wall.
My dilemma was whether to tell my friend about the spinach in her teeth.

confused.note: A dilemma is specifically a hard choice between options, not just any problem.

questions.passage: The discovery placed the museum in a ______. If it announced that its most famous painting was a forgery, attendance would collapse; if it kept silent, it would be deceiving every visitor.
questions.explanation: Two options, each with a serious cost, make a difficult choice.

distractors.why: A stimulus is something that prompts action, not a hard choice.
A culmination is a final high point, which does not fit.
A hierarchy is a system of ranks, which does not fit.

definition: to officially forbid something

examples.text: The law prohibited the export of grain during the famine.
Safety rules prohibit eating or drinking in the laboratory.
The pool prohibits running, diving, and my uncle's cannonballs.

confused.note: To prohibit is to forbid by rule; to inhibit is to hold back or slow down.

questions.passage: Rules at the nature reserve ______ visitors from leaving the marked trails. Rangers explain that a single footstep can crush plants that take decades to grow back.
questions.explanation: The rules forbid leaving the trails.

distractors.why: Prescribe means to order or recommend, and "prescribe visitors from" is not how it is used.
Supplant means to replace, which does not fit.
Quell means to put down or calm, which does not fit rules and trails.

partsNote: from Latin habere, "to hold": to hold back

definition: a person who is new to an activity and has little experience

examples.text: The guild required every novice to train for seven years.
Even a novice can spot Saturn's rings through a small telescope.
I am a novice at skiing, as the bruises prove.

confused.note: A novice is a beginner; novel means new, or a book of fiction.

questions.passage: The climbing school pairs each ______ with an experienced guide. Beginners are not allowed on the upper wall until they have shown, over at least ten sessions, that they can tie every knot from memory.
questions.explanation: Someone who must learn the basics is a beginner.

distractors.why: A proponent is a supporter of a cause, not a beginner.
A virtuoso is a master, the opposite of someone still learning knots.
A sycophant is a flatterer, which does not fit.

definition: the final result or highest point of something, after a long time

examples.text: The treaty was the culmination of four years of secret talks.
The launch was the culmination of a decade of design and testing.
The spring concert is the culmination of months of rehearsals.

confused.note: A culmination is a crowning end point; a termination is simply an ending.

questions.passage: The publication of the dictionary in 1928 was the ______ of seventy years of work. Six editors had led the project in turn, and two of them had died before seeing a single finished volume.
questions.explanation: A final result reached after seventy years is a culmination.

distractors.why: An onset is a beginning, the opposite of a final result.
A quirk is an odd habit or feature, which does not fit.
An altercation is a noisy quarrel, which does not fit.

definition: to prevent someone from moving or progressing easily

examples.text: Heavy rain hampered efforts to map the flooded valley.
A shortage of horses hampered the army's advance.
A sprained wrist hampered my typing for a week.

confused.note: To hamper is to hinder; to pamper is to spoil with comfort.

questions.passage: Firefighters reached the blaze within minutes, but their work was ______ by a lack of water. The nearest hydrant had been damaged, and hoses had to be run from a pond half a mile away.
questions.explanation: A lack of water made their work harder.

distractors.why: Abetted means helped, the opposite of what the water shortage did.
Flaunted means showed off, which does not fit.
Debased means lowered in quality or value, which does not describe slowed firefighting.

definition: causing harm gradually and secretly, so that it is not noticed until too late

examples.text: The disease is insidious, showing no symptoms for years.
The insidious spread of bribery hollowed out the courts.
The insidious thing about that app is how an hour vanishes without my noticing.

confused.note: Insidious means harmful in a hidden, gradual way; invidious means likely to cause resentment.

questions.passage: Carbon monoxide is especially ______ because it gives no warning. The gas has no color, smell, or taste, and victims often feel only a mild headache before losing consciousness.
questions.explanation: A danger that gives no warning harms gradually and unnoticed.

distractors.why: Strident means loud and harsh, the opposite of something that gives no warning.
Rudimentary means basic, which does not describe a hidden danger.
Posthumous means after death, which does not fit.

definition: a noisy argument or disagreement

examples.text: An altercation between two officers delayed the regiment's departure.
The dinner ends with an altercation over who inherited the piano.
There was a brief altercation in the parking lot over the last space.

confused.note: An altercation is a quarrel; an alteration is a change.

questions.passage: What began as a polite disagreement about a referee's call soon became a heated ______. The two coaches stood nose to nose, shouting, until officials stepped between them.
questions.explanation: Coaches shouting nose to nose is a noisy argument.

distractors.why: A culmination is a final high point, which does not describe a quarrel.
An alteration is a change; it only resembles the right word.
Credulity is readiness to believe, which does not fit.

definition: in very bad condition because of neglect; abandoned

examples.text: After the mine closed, the town's hotel stood derelict for fifty years.
The children explore a derelict lighthouse at the end of the bay.
The derelict gas station on the corner is finally being torn down.

confused.note: Derelict means abandoned or neglected; delinquent means failing in a duty or behind on a payment.

questions.passage: The city has announced plans to convert the ______ warehouse into apartments. Empty since 1980, the building has broken windows, a collapsed roof, and trees growing through its upper floors.
questions.explanation: A long-empty building with a collapsed roof is abandoned and in ruins.

distractors.why: Pristine means in perfect condition, the opposite of this warehouse.
Indelible means impossible to remove, which does not describe a ruined building.
Ardent means passionate, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin linquere, "to leave": left behind

definition: to stop something, such as violence, fear, or protest, often by force

examples.text: The governor called in troops to quell the riots.
The spray quells the itching within a minute.
A glass of water quelled my hiccups at last.

confused.note: To quell is to put down or calm; a quill is a feather pen.

questions.passage: Rumors that the bank was about to fail sent hundreds of customers to its doors. To ______ the panic, the manager stacked cash in the front window and announced that every withdrawal would be paid in full.
questions.explanation: Showing the cash was meant to stop the panic.

distractors.why: Foment means to stir up, the opposite of calming a panic.
Flaunt means to show off; he displayed the cash, but what he did to the panic was calm it.
Equivocate means to speak evasively, which cannot take "the panic" as an object.

definition: impossible to remove or forget

examples.text: The famine left an indelible mark on the nation's memory.
The dye leaves an indelible stain on the cell wall.
My little cousin drew on the couch with indelible marker.

confused.note: Indelible means impossible to erase; inedible means not fit to eat.

questions.passage: The teacher made an ______ impression on her students. Fifty years later, many could still recite the poems she had taught them and recall the exact words she used to praise their work.
questions.explanation: An impression still vivid after fifty years cannot be erased.

distractors.why: Fleeting means lasting only a moment, the opposite of fifty years.
Abysmal means extremely bad, which the students' fond memories contradict.
Rudimentary means basic, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin delere, "to destroy": not able to be wiped out

definition: to destroy something completely so that nothing remains

examples.text: The eruption obliterated the town in a single afternoon.
A large asteroid impact could obliterate most life on the planet.
The rain obliterated our chalk drawings within minutes.

confused.note: To obliterate is to destroy; to obligate is to bind by duty.

questions.passage: Archaeologists had hoped to find the foundations of the old fort. They discovered instead that a quarry dug on the site in the 1800s had ______ every trace of it.
questions.explanation: The quarry destroyed the fort so completely that nothing remained.

distractors.why: Hampered means hindered, far too weak for removing every trace.
Fomented means stirred up, which does not fit.
Ousted means forced someone out of a position, which does not apply to traces of a fort.

partsNote: from Latin littera, "letter": to strike out the letters

definition: loud, harsh, and unpleasant; or expressing opinions forcefully

examples.text: The strident whistle of the factory wakes the whole valley.
The pamphlet's strident tone alienated readers who might have agreed with it.
The strident alarm on my phone could wake the neighbors.

confused.note: Strident means harsh and loud; stringent means strict.

questions.passage: The reformer's early speeches were calm and reasoned. As years passed without change, her language grew more ______, and she began denouncing her opponents by name as "thieves" and "cowards."
questions.explanation: Calling opponents thieves and cowards is harsh, forceful language.

distractors.why: Decorous means polite and restrained, which describes her earlier manner.
Posthumous means occurring after death, which does not fit.
Derelict means abandoned, which does not describe language.

definition: having bad habits that cannot be changed or improved

examples.text: The incorrigible prankster puts a frog in the bishop's hat.
The court declared him an incorrigible smuggler and banished him.
My grandfather is an incorrigible tease.

confused.note: Incorrigible means unable to be reformed; incorruptible means unable to be bribed.

questions.passage: Teachers had tried warnings, detentions, and long talks, all without effect. The boy was an ______ daydreamer who, within minutes of any lesson's start, would be gazing out the window at the clouds.
questions.explanation: A habit that no measure can change is beyond correction.

distractors.why: Ardent means passionate; the stress here is that nothing could change him.
Penitent means remorseful and ready to reform, which he was not.
Indelible means impossible to erase, a word for marks and memories, not people.

partsNote: from Latin regere, "to guide": not able to be set right

definition: to help or encourage someone to do something wrong

examples.text: The innkeeper was hanged for abetting the smugglers.
The maid abets the elopement by leaving the garden gate unlocked.
My sister abetted my cookie theft by distracting Mom.

confused.note: Abet means to help in wrongdoing; abate means to lessen.

questions.passage: The clerk did not steal the money himself. He was convicted of ______ the theft, however, because he had told the robbers when the safe would be open and had switched off the alarm.
questions.explanation: Giving information and disabling the alarm helped the crime.

distractors.why: Abating means lessening; it resembles the right word but does not mean helping.
Quelling means suppressing, the opposite of helping a theft.
Decrying means condemning, which he did not do.

definition: to cause or encourage trouble, anger, or rebellion

examples.text: Spies were sent to foment unrest in the border towns.
The jealous brother foments suspicion between the king and his heir.
My cousin loves to foment arguments at dinner and then sit back and watch.

confused.note: To foment is to stir up trouble; to ferment is to undergo a chemical change, as in making bread or wine.

questions.passage: The pamphlets were not meant to inform. Their authors hoped to ______ rebellion, and each page urged readers to refuse the new tax and to drive the king's collectors from their towns.
questions.explanation: Urging readers to resist and expel collectors is stirring up rebellion.

distractors.why: Quell means to put down, the opposite of urging rebellion.
Oust means to remove someone from a position; one stirs up a rebellion, one does not remove it.
Fathom means to understand, which was not the authors' aim.

definition: wildly wasteful with money or resources

examples.text: The profligate court spent more on fireworks than on the navy.
The profligate uncle gambles away the family silver.
Leaving every light on is a profligate use of electricity.

confused.note: Profligate means wildly wasteful; prolific means highly productive.

questions.passage: The audit described the agency's spending as ______. In one year it had bought four hundred computers for a staff of ninety and paid for a conference at a beach resort that only eleven people attended.
questions.explanation: Buying far more than needed is wildly wasteful.

distractors.why: Frugal means careful with money, the opposite of this spending.
Prolific means highly productive; it looks similar but does not mean wasteful.
Insidious means harmful in a hidden way; this waste was obvious.

definition: angry bitterness in speech or manner

examples.text: The debate over the treaty was marked by unusual acrimony.
The partners dissolve their firm with surprising acrimony.
The game of charades ended in acrimony over a disputed clue.

confused.note: Acrimony is bitterness; alimony is money paid to a former spouse.

questions.passage: The two authors had once been close friends, but their dispute over credit for the book ended in ______. Each published an article attacking the other, and they never spoke again.
questions.explanation: Public attacks and a permanent break show angry bitterness.

distractors.why: Adulation is excessive praise, the opposite of attacking each other.
Credulity is readiness to believe, which does not fit.
A culmination is a final high point, which does not capture the bitterness.

definition: a tendency to believe things too easily

examples.text: Swindlers grew rich on the credulity of investors in the scheme.
The tale strains the reader's credulity with its talking horse.
My credulity has limits, and "the dog did my homework" is past them.

confused.note: Credulity is readiness to believe too easily; credibility is the quality of being believable.

questions.passage: The magician depended on the ______ of his audience. Few stopped to ask how a man who claimed he could turn lead into gold had come to be performing in a rented tent for a few coins.
questions.explanation: An audience that does not question an unlikely claim believes too easily.

distractors.why: Acrimony is bitterness, which is not what the magician relied on.
Skepticism is doubt, the opposite of unquestioning belief.
Credibility is believability; the audience's readiness to believe is credulity.

definition: a person who is new to a subject, skill, or belief

examples.text: The senate's neophytes were expected to listen for a year before speaking.
The telescope is simple enough for a neophyte to use.
As a cooking neophyte, I once set off the smoke alarm making toast.

confused.note: A neophyte is a beginner; an acolyte is a devoted assistant or follower.

questions.passage: Chess clubs welcome ______ as well as experts. New members who have never moved a pawn are paired with patient volunteers and are not entered in tournaments until they ask to be.
questions.explanation: Members who have never played are beginners.

distractors.why: Virtuosos are masters of a skill, the opposite of those who have never played.
Proponents are supporters of a cause, not beginners.
Quirks are odd habits, not people.

definition: to reduce the quality, value, or dignity of something

examples.text: The king debased the coinage by mixing copper into the silver.
The critic argues that the sequel debases everything fine in the original.
Do not debase a good pizza with cold canned pineapple.

confused.note: To debase is to lower in quality; to debate is to argue formally.

questions.passage: Purists complained that the new edition ______ the dictionary. By admitting slang, abbreviations, and words borrowed from advertising, they argued, the editors had lowered the standards of a great reference work.
questions.explanation: Lowering the standards reduces the work's quality and dignity.

distractors.why: Ousted means removed from a position, which does not fit a dictionary.
Quelled means suppressed, which does not fit.
Abetted means helped in wrongdoing, which does not fit.

partsNote: to bring down from the base

definition: to speak in a vague or unclear way in order to avoid the truth or a commitment

examples.text: Asked whether he would sign the treaty, the envoy equivocated for an hour.
The witness equivocates, and the detective knows she is hiding something.
When I asked who broke the lamp, my brother equivocated about "strong winds."

confused.note: To equivocate is to speak evasively; equivalent means equal in value.

questions.passage: Pressed to say whether the factory would close, the spokesman chose to ______. "All options remain open," he said, and "we value every employee," but he would not answer yes or no.
questions.explanation: Vague phrases in place of a yes or no are evasive speech.

distractors.why: Hamper means to hinder, and it needs an object; it does not mean speaking evasively.
Obliterate means to destroy completely, which does not fit.
Flaunt means to show off, which does not fit.

partsNote: to speak equally on both sides

definition: very enthusiastic or passionate

examples.text: She was an ardent supporter of votes for women.
The poet's ardent letters fill three volumes.
My dad is an ardent fan of a team that has not won in decades.

confused.note: Ardent means passionate; arduous means very difficult.

questions.passage: Few people care much about typefaces, but Lena is an ______ admirer of them. She can name the designer of nearly any font, collects old printing manuals, and once traveled to another country to see a rare set of metal type.
questions.explanation: Collecting manuals and traveling abroad for type show passionate enthusiasm.

distractors.why: Derelict means neglected or abandoned, which does not describe an admirer.
Abysmal means extremely bad, which does not fit.
Incorrigible suggests a bad habit that cannot be fixed, the wrong tone for a harmless enthusiasm.

definition: basic and simple; not fully developed

examples.text: The early mammal had only rudimentary eyes, little more than light-sensitive spots.
The settlers built rudimentary shelters of bark and mud.
My Spanish is rudimentary: I can order tacos and apologize.

confused.note: Rudimentary is the adjective; the rudiments of a subject are its first, basic principles.

questions.passage: By modern standards, the first computers had only ______ memory. A machine that filled an entire room could store fewer characters than a single modern text message.
questions.explanation: Memory smaller than a text message is basic and undeveloped.

distractors.why: Indelible means impossible to erase, which is not what the comparison shows.
Insidious means harmful in a hidden way, which does not fit.
Strident means loud and harsh, which does not fit.

definition: an unusual habit or feature; a strange chance event

examples.text: A quirk of the planet's orbit gives it seasons that last twenty years.
The detective's quirks include a refusal to wear matching socks.
One quirk of our old car is that the radio works only when the wipers are on.

confused.note: A quirk is an oddity; a quark is a subatomic particle.

questions.passage: By a ______ of the calendar, the school's hundredth anniversary fell on the same day as the final match of the national tournament, and the planned ceremony had to compete with a stadium full of fans next door.
questions.explanation: Two events landing on the same day by chance is an odd accident.

distractors.why: A culmination is a final high point, not a chance coincidence.
A neophyte is a beginner, which does not fit.
Credulity is readiness to believe, which does not fit.

definition: happening, awarded, or published after a person's death

examples.text: The soldier received a posthumous medal for bravery.
The poet's fame is entirely posthumous; she published nothing while alive.
The band released a posthumous album of the singer's unfinished songs.

confused.note: Posthumous means after death; posterior means at the back.

questions.passage: During his lifetime the painter sold only one canvas. His recognition was ______: within twenty years of his death, museums on three continents were competing to buy his work.
questions.explanation: Fame that arrived after he died came after death.

distractors.why: Rudimentary means basic, which does not describe when recognition came.
Strident means loud and harsh, which does not fit.
Ardent means passionate; the colon explains timing, not intensity.

definition: to force someone out of a position or place

examples.text: The generals ousted the president in a bloodless coup.
The younger brother schemes to oust the heir from the castle.
I was ousted from the couch by a very large dog.

confused.note: To oust is to force out; to joust is to fight on horseback with lances.

questions.passage: After three years of falling profits, shareholders voted to ______ the company's founder. She was replaced as chief executive by a manager hired from a rival firm.
questions.explanation: Voting her out and replacing her is forcing her from the position.

distractors.why: Abet means to help in wrongdoing, which does not fit.
Debase means to lower in quality, which does not describe removing someone.
Exonerate means to clear of blame, which is not what the vote did.

definition: extremely bad

examples.text: Conditions in the prison ships were abysmal.
The first prototype had an abysmal success rate of one launch in twenty.
The service was abysmal: we waited an hour for cold soup.

confused.note: Abysmal means extremely bad; abyssal relates to the deep ocean floor.

questions.passage: The team's record last season was ______. It lost twenty-eight of thirty games, was outscored by an average of forty points, and set a league record for fewest fans in attendance.
questions.explanation: Losing twenty-eight of thirty games is an extremely bad record.

distractors.why: Exemplary means serving as a model, the opposite of this record.
Posthumous means after death, which does not fit.
Insidious means harmful in a hidden way; this failure was plain to see.

definition: to show off something in a way meant to attract attention or envy

examples.text: The banker flaunted his wealth with a carriage plated in silver.
She flaunts her new ring at every table in the tea room.
My brother flaunted his driver's license for a week after passing the test.

confused.note: To flaunt is to show off; to flout is to openly disobey a rule.

questions.passage: Unlike neighbors who kept their fortunes quiet, the oil baron ______ his. He built a marble mansion on the highest hill in town and drove a different imported car each day of the week.
questions.explanation: A mansion on a hill and a car for each day are wealth shown off.

distractors.why: Flouted means defied a rule; wealth is flaunted, not flouted.
Quelled means suppressed, the opposite of displaying.
Debased means lowered in value, which is not what he did with his fortune.
